blocks.title: Demand and the law of demand
blocks.md: **Demand** is the quantity of a good that consumers are **willing and able to buy** at each price in a given period. The **law of demand**: as the price falls, the quantity demanded rises, and as the price rises, the quantity demanded falls (other things being equal). A **demand schedule** is a table and a **demand curve** is its graph; it slopes downwards.

blocks.title: Movement and shift
blocks.md: A change in the **price of the good** causes a **movement along** the curve: an **extension** (price falls) or a **contraction** (price rises) of quantity demanded. A change in a **condition of demand** shifts the whole curve: **increase** (right) or **decrease** (left). Conditions: income, tastes and fashion, prices of related goods, population, advertising and expectations.

blocks.caption: Demand curves D1 and D2: an increase in demand shifts the whole curve to the right.
blocks.alt: Two parallel downward-sloping lines, the second to the right of the first.

blocks.title: Do not mix the two changes
blocks.md: Never say 'demand rises' when only the price has fallen: that is a rise in **quantity demanded**. Never draw a shift for a price change. Substitutes (garri and rice) have a **positive** link: a dearer substitute raises demand. Complements (cars and fuel) have a **negative** link: a dearer complement lowers demand for the other.

blocks.title: Normal and inferior goods
blocks.md: For a **normal good**, a rise in income raises demand. For an **inferior good** (a cheap, low-quality substitute that people drop when they can afford better), a rise in income lowers demand. **Market demand** is the sum of all individual demands at each price.

blocks.title: Worked example — reading a schedule
blocks.statement: At a market in Mbouda the demand for tomatoes is 20 kg at 600 FCFA per kg and 40 kg at 400 FCFA per kg (illustrative). Describe the change and name it.
steps: The price falls from 600 to 400 FCFA.
Quantity demanded rises from 20 kg to 40 kg.
This is an extension of demand: a movement along the same demand curve, not a shift.
blocks.answer: Extension of demand (movement along the curve)

blocks.title: Worked example — market demand
blocks.statement: Three households demand 4, 6 and 5 loaves a day at 200 FCFA each. Find the market demand for the three households, then say what happens if bread becomes a fashion in the town.
steps: A change in fashion is a change in tastes, a condition of demand.
So demand increases at every price: the curve shifts to the right.
blocks.answer: 15 loaves; the demand curve shifts right

blocks.title: Supply and the law of supply
blocks.md: **Supply** is the quantity of a good that producers are **willing and able to offer for sale** at each price in a given period. The **law of supply**: as the price rises, the quantity supplied rises (producers earn more per unit and new producers enter), and as the price falls, quantity supplied falls. The **supply curve** slopes upwards.

blocks.title: Movement and shift
blocks.md: A change in the **price of the good** causes a **movement along** the curve (an **extension** or a **contraction** of supply). A change in a **condition of supply** shifts the whole curve: **increase** (right) or **decrease** (left). Conditions: costs of production (wages, raw materials, rent), technology, weather (for farm goods), taxes and subsidies, prices of other goods that producers could make.

blocks.caption: Supply curves S1 and S2: a fall in costs shifts the supply curve to the right (S1 to S2, drawn as the lower line).
blocks.alt: Two parallel upward-sloping lines, the second lower and to the right.

blocks.title: Taxes and subsidies
blocks.md: A **tax** on producers raises costs and shifts supply to the **left**; a **subsidy** lowers costs and shifts it to the **right**. Better technology also shifts supply to the right. Do not confuse these with a change in the price of the product itself, which only moves producers along the same curve.

blocks.title: Why supply is slow to change
blocks.md: Farm supply is slow because crops take months to grow, and perishable goods cannot be stored easily. Supply of some goods can be raised quickly (sold from stock) while others need new machines or land; so the time period matters. **Market supply** is the sum of all firms' supplies at each price.

blocks.title: Worked example — reading a schedule
blocks.statement: A farmer in Bafoussam supplies 20 kg of beans at 400 FCFA per kg and 30 kg at 500 FCFA per kg (illustrative). Describe the change.
steps: The price rises from 400 to 500 FCFA.
Quantity supplied rises from 20 kg to 30 kg.
This is an extension of supply: a movement along the same supply curve.

blocks.title: Worked example — a shift
blocks.statement: The government subsidises fertiliser for maize growers in the North West. What happens to the supply curve and why?
steps: A subsidy lowers the farmer's cost of production.
Farmers can now supply more maize at every price.
The supply curve shifts to the right: an increase in supply.

blocks.title: Equilibrium
blocks.md: The **equilibrium price** is the price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied. It is where the demand and supply curves cross. If the price is **too high** there is a **surplus**, so sellers lower the price; if **too low** there is a **shortage**, so buyers bid the price up. The price mechanism pushes the market to equilibrium.

blocks.title: Effects of shifts
blocks.md: **Demand rises** (curve right): price rises and quantity rises. **Demand falls**: price and quantity fall. **Supply rises** (curve right): price falls and quantity rises. **Supply falls**: price rises and quantity falls. Always **draw** the shift first, then read the new price and quantity; change only **one** curve at a time.

blocks.caption: Equilibrium at E, where demand and supply cross (Q = 4.5, P = 11 hundred FCFA).
blocks.alt: A downward demand line and an upward supply line crossing at point E with dotted guide lines to the axes.

blocks.title: Price control
blocks.md: A **maximum price** (price ceiling) is set below equilibrium to protect buyers, but it causes a **shortage**, queues and black markets. A **minimum price** (price floor) is set above equilibrium to protect producers, such as farmers, but it causes a **surplus** that someone must buy or store. Price controls are used on some staple goods in many countries.

blocks.title: Frequent errors
blocks.md: Do not say 'the price is where demand equals supply' without 'quantity'. A shortage is measured by **demand minus supply** at the controlled price, a surplus by **supply minus demand**. A price rise after a demand increase is a movement along the supply curve, not a shift of supply.

blocks.title: Worked example — equilibrium
blocks.statement: In a local market the demand for garri is P = 20 − 2Q and the supply is P = 2 + 2Q, where P is in hundreds of FCFA and Q in kg (illustrative). Find the equilibrium.
steps: At equilibrium demand price equals supply price: 20 − 2Q = 2 + 2Q.
P = 20 − 2 × 4.5 = 11 hundred FCFA, so the price is 1 100 FCFA.

blocks.title: Worked example — a maximum price
blocks.statement: Using the same market, the authorities fix a maximum price of 600 FCFA, that is P = 6. Find the shortage.
